title: The present tense
intro: This unit brings the first verb tense: the present in `-ýAr`. It says what is happening now, what happens regularly and what is planned soon. You will learn to find a verb's stem, add the tense and the personal endings, make the tense negative, and ask questions with it.

blocks.text: A dictionary lists a verb in its infinitive, which ends in *-mak* after a back vowel and *-mek* after a front one: *okamak* (to read), *gelmek* (to come). Take that ending off and you have the stem, the part every verb form is built on: *oka-*, *gel-*. In the guides a stem is written with a hyphen after it.
Some stems end in a consonant (*gel-*, *ýaz-*, *garaş-*), some in a vowel (*oka-*, *işle-*, *ýaşa-*), and a few in *ý* (*iý-*, *söý-*). That matters when endings join them, as the next section shows.
Verbs made of two words, such as *pikir etmek* (to think) or *kömek etmek* (to help), change only their last word: *pikir edýärin*, I think.

blocks.title: Keep the stem's vowel
blocks.text: Take off the whole *-mak* or *-mek*. The *a* in *oka-mak* and the *e* in *işle-mek* belong to the stem: *okaýar*, *işleýär*, never `okýar` or `işlýär`.

To say what someone **is doing** or **does**, add `-ýAr` to the stem: *-ýar* after a back vowel, *-ýär* after a front one. Note the *ä*: in this tense the front form is *ä*, not *e*. Then add an ending for the person. With no ending, it is **he**, **she** or **it**: *gelýär*, she comes.

These are the same endings you saw after `-dYr` in the formal **to be** of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *talypdyryn*, *gelýärin*. With *olar*, the *-lAr* can be left out when the pronoun is said: *Olar işleýär* or *Olar işleýärler*.

**Stems ending in a vowel** take `-ýAr` straight on, and keep their vowel: *oka-* → *okaýar*, *işle-* → *işleýär*, *ýaşa-* → *ýaşaýar*. **Stems ending in ý** keep it too, so two *ý* meet: *iý-* → *iýýär*, *söý-* → *söýýär*.

**t becomes d.** A short list of verbs ending in *t* change it to *d* before `-ýAr`. In this unit: *gitmek* → *gidýär*, *etmek* → *edýär*, *aýtmak* → *aýdýar* (says) and *öwretmek* → *öwredýär* (teaches); verbs made with *etmek* follow it: *pikir edýär*. Most verbs in *t* keep it: *ýatmak* → *ýatýar* (lies down), *satmak* → *satýar* (sells).

blocks.text: **The pronoun can go.** The ending already says who, so the pronoun is optional, unlike with **to be** in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *Okaýaryn* means **I'm reading** on its own. Say *Men okaýaryn* to stress **I**.

blocks.title: ä, not e
blocks.text: Write *-ýär* with *ä*: *gelýär*, *işleýär*, never `gelýer`. And a stem in a vowel keeps that vowel: *okaýar*, not `okýar`.

To make a verb negative, put `-mA` (*-ma* or *-me*) between the stem and `-ýAr`: *gel-me-ýär*, he isn't coming; *oka-ma-ýar*, she isn't reading. With verbs, **not** is this ending, not *däl*. A *t* that becomes *d* stays *t* before *-mA*: *gitmeýär*, *etmeýär*.

**Questions.** Add `-mY` after the personal ending, all in one word: *Gelýärsiňmi?* Are you coming? *Okaýarmy?* Is she reading? With *sen* and *siz* you will also hear the particle **before** the ending: *gelýärmiň?*, *gelýärmisiňiz?* Both are right; this course writes the first.

blocks.title: In speech
blocks.text: Everyday speech shortens many forms: *gelýän* for *gelýärin*, and a common spoken negative is *Men bilemok*, I don't know. You will hear these; this course writes the standard forms.

blocks.title: Still one word
blocks.text: The particle is written onto the verb, after the ending: *gelýärsiňmi*, not `gelýärsiň mi`.

The `-ýAr` present covers more ground than one English tense. It says what is happening **now**, what happens **regularly**, and what is **planned** for the near future. Time words make the meaning clear.

items.en: Right now Aýna is reading a book.

blocks.text: Time words usually come early in the sentence, before the verb, and can go before or after the subject: *Men şu gün işleýärin* or *Şu gün men işleýärin*. The verb stays at the end.

blocks.title: One tense, three English ones
blocks.text: *Men çaý içýärin* can be **I drink tea**, **I'm drinking tea** or **I'm going to drink tea**. English has to choose; Turkmen leaves it to the time words and the situation.
Turkmen has a second present, for general truths and habits, which you will meet in [A2 unit 4](a2-u04). Until then, `-ýAr` is right for all of these.

summary: The stem is the infinitive without *-mak* or *-mek*: *oka-*, *gel-*, *işle-*.
The present is stem + `-ýAr` (*-ýar*, or *-ýär* with *ä*) + a personal ending: *-Yn, -sYň, —, -Ys, -sYňYz, -lAr*: *okaýaryn, gelýärsiň, işleýär*.
A few verbs change *t* to *d* before it: *gidýär, edýär, aýdýar, öwredýär*; most keep it: *satýar*.
The ending says who, so the pronoun can be left out: *Okaýaryn*.
Negative: `-mA` before `-ýAr`: *bilmeýärin*. Question: `-mY` after the ending: *gelýärsiňmi?* (also *gelýärmiň?*)
One present for now, habits and plans: *häzir*, *her gün*, *ertir* make it clear.
